To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
skin fibroblastic cells from various hereditary cancers exhibit impaired DNA repair capacity.
skin fibroblastic cells from various hereditary syndromes exhibit an impaired capacity to repair UV-induced DNA damage.

cells from patients with the hereditary cancer-proneness syndromes, aniridia, Li-Fraumenis, dysplastic nev syndrome, Von Hippel-Linda syndrome and breast/ovarian syndrome, display impaired capacity to repair damaged DNA, and that the repair defect in cells from the breast/ovary syndrome is not restricted to the cells of the patients but also to cells from their healthy relatives.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms of DNA repair and its regulation, and the role of DNA repair in carcinogenesis.
the role of the DNA repair system in the development of hereditary cancer syndromes.
the role of defective DNA repair in the etiology of cancer-prone syndrromes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a general defect in the repair of UV-induced DNA damage in skin fibroblast cells derived from patients with various hereditary cancer syndromes.
the DNA repair capacity in cells from cancer-prone individuals is reduced, and that the reduced capacity is associated with an increased risk of cancer.
the DNA repair defect in the hereditary cancer syndromes is not due to the specific mutation in a particular tumor-suppressor gene but rather to the presence of an inherited cancer syndrome itself.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cells from cancer-prone individuals with mutations in tumor-suppressor genes have reduced DNA repair capacity, which may predispose to cancer.
the DNA repair capacity of cells from cancer-prone individuals is reduced, but the mechanism of the impairment is unknown.
there is a relationship between impaired DNA repair and cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cells from patients with cancer-prone syndomes show a reduced ability to repair DNA damage.
the repair capacity of the cells in these cancer-prone syndrromes may be impaired.
